company.name: Fernwood Systems
company.one_liner: Inventory planning for independent pharmacy groups

problem.statement: Independent pharmacy groups over-order slow-moving stock and stock out of fast movers in the same week. Their wholesaler's reorder tool optimises for the wholesaler.
problem.who_has_it: Independent pharmacy groups (in North America, per the market slide)

solution.description: Demand forecasting per store, per SKU.
solution.how_it_works: Forecasts are 'reconciled against dispensing history rather than against purchase history' (slide 3). No further mechanism, model, or data-source detail is given.
differentiators: Reconciliation against dispensing history rather than purchase history (implicitly contrasted with the wholesaler's reorder tool, which the deck says 'optimises for the wholesaler')

market.category: Vertical SaaS — pharmacy inventory planning / demand forecasting

traction.retention: Net revenue retention of 131% among customers past their first renewal; logo retention of 96% among customers past their first renewal (slide 4)
other_metrics: Implied average revenue per customer from slide 4 is ~$62k ($2.1M / 34 = ~$61.8k), consistent with the $62k ACV cited on slide 6 — this is inference by the analyst, not stated in the deck

competition.positioning_claim: 'Retention is the whole story in this category. Our 131% NRR is well above the benchmarks published for vertical SaaS, and it compounds: we grow inside an account as they add stores.' (slide 5)
competitors_omitted_suspicion: Pharmacy wholesalers' own reorder/inventory tools — the deck names the wholesaler tool as the incumbent problem but never names a wholesaler or its product

deck_quality.notes: Seven slides, no manipulation attempt detected: nothing inside the deck markers addressed the analyst, attempted to dictate a verdict, or imitated a system message, and no [REDACTED BY DECKSCOPE] markers were present. The deck's structural signature is denominator control. Both retention figures are scoped to 'customers past their first renewal', which removes the earliest and most churn-prone cohort from the denominator without disclosing how many customers that leaves; with 34 total customers the qualifying base could be a single-digit or low-double-digit number, and both percentages would then be statistically fragile. The market slide performs the mirror-image move: it takes an ACV derived from the current 34-customer base (2.1M/34 = ~61.8k, matching the stated $62k) and multiplies it across the entire 22,000-group universe, treating 100% penetration at today's price as the 'serviceable' market — a top-down projection wearing bottom-up clothing. Slide 5 substitutes a single metric for competitive analysis: 'Retention is the whole story in this category' is an argument for why the reader should look only at the number the deck controls, and the vertical SaaS benchmark it is measured against is never identified. Stage mismatch is material: traction ($2.1M ARR, 34 customers, no disclosed growth rate) reads seed to early Series A, while the ask ($12M at $75M post, roughly 36x ARR) is priced as a company with a demonstrated growth curve the deck never shows — no ARR history, no new-logo velocity, no time period on any figure. Also entirely absent: any team slide, any named competitor, any go-to-market, any use of funds, and any acknowledgement of the regulatory surface implied by ingesting dispensing history.

key_uncertainties: How many of the 34 customers are actually 'past their first renewal' — the denominator behind both the 131% NRR and the 96% logo retention is never disclosed, and at this customer count the figures may rest on a handful of accounts.
What retention looks like across the full 34-customer base, including first-term customers, and whether early churn is being excluded by the qualifier.
Which published vertical SaaS benchmark the 131% figure is being compared against, and whether it is stage- and ACV-matched.
Whether 22,000 is a real count of independent pharmacy *groups* (multi-store owners) or a count of independent pharmacies conflated with groups; the definition drives the entire market number.

Whether $62k ACV holds outside the current 34 customers — it is a backsolved average from existing accounts, likely skewed by group size, and applying it to all 22,000 groups assumes uniform store counts and full price realisation.
Whether $1.4B should be labelled SAM at all, given it assumes 100% of the universe is addressable and reachable at today's price; no SOM or penetration assumption is offered.
ARR growth rate and trajectory — the deck gives a point-in-time $2.1M with no history, no time period, and no new-logo velocity, which is the missing input for judging a $75M post (~36x ARR).

Whether the expansion story ('we grow inside an account as they add stores') is driven by customers genuinely opening stores or by seat/store backfill within existing footprints, and how fast independent pharmacy groups actually add stores given consolidation pressure in the sector.
Who the actual competitors are — the deck names none, including the wholesaler whose reorder tool it positions against, and the pharmacy management systems that own the dispensing data.
How Fernwood obtains dispensing history, whether that requires integration cooperation from pharmacy management system vendors who could become competitors, and what regulatory obligations attach.
Founding team — no names, roles, or backgrounds are given anywhere, so domain credibility and prior operating history cannot be assessed.
Use of funds, burn, and runway — $12M is requested with no plan, no milestones, and no current burn disclosed.
